extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in combinatorics/graph theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and proofs around list-coloring problems (the Dinitz problem and Galvin's solution), related lemmas (kernels, stable matchings), the 5-list-colorability of planar graphs, plus the art-gallery (n/3 guards) theorem. Focus is on constructive proofs and sufficient conditions for list-colorings and completions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smetaniuk's theorem (completion of partial Latin squares)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any partial Latin square of order n with at most n − 1 filled cells can be completed to a Latin square of the same order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on n: permute rows/columns to put filled cells below diagonal with a unique occurrence of one symbol on the diagonal; remove that symbol and apply induction to n−1; then perform a sequence of controlled exchanges between a column k and the last column, analyzed by a bipartite graph G_k to avoid infinite loops. The proof gives an explicit constructive completion (reverse the permutations at the end). Examples and an illustrated run-through are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: kernel of a directed graph
rubrics_metrics.description: A kernel K ⊆ V in a directed graph (V,E) is a set of vertices such that (i) K is independent (no edges within K), and (ii) for every u ∉ K there exists a vertex v ∈ K with an arc u → v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a combinatorial object in proofs about list-colorings: kernels allow picking a color common to a set of vertices and removing them while preserving an outdegree vs. list-size inequality. Example: {b,c,f} can constitute a kernel in a small directed graph; a 3-cycle may have no kernel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (kernel condition implies list coloring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let G be a directed graph. If for each vertex v we have a color set C(v) with |C(v)| ≥ d+(v) + 1, and every induced subgraph of G possesses a kernel, then there exists a list coloring choosing for each v a color from C(v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction: choose a color c and let A(c) = {v : c ∈ C(v)}; take a kernel K(c) in the induced subgraph on A(c), color K(c) with c, delete K(c) and c from lists; outdegrees in A(c)\,K(c) drop by at least 1 so the inequality still holds, continue inductively. This gives a constructive reduction strategy for list-colorings when kernels exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/criterion: list chromatic number χ_l(G)
rubrics_metrics.description: χ_l(G) is the smallest k such that for any assignment of lists C(v) with |C(v)| = k for all v there exists a list coloring c with c(v) ∈ C(v) for all v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relation: χ(G) ≤ χ_l(G). Examples show χ_l(G) can be strictly larger than χ(G) (e.g., K2,4 has χ=2 but χ_l ≥ 3); line graphs and special constructions are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2 (existence of stable matching — Gale–Shapley)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any bipartite graph with complete preference rankings on neighbor sets, a stable matching exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by the deferred acceptance algorithm: men propose to top choices iteratively; women keep best current proposal; rejected men propose to next choices until reservoir empty. The resulting matching is stable because any blocking pair would contradict the rejection history. Stable matchings are used to produce kernels in associated induced subgraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galvin's theorem (Dinitz problem): χ_l(S_n) = n
rubrics_metrics.description: For the n×n square graph S_n (cells adjacent if in same row or column) the list chromatic number equals n: χ_l(S_n) = n, i.e., the Dinitz problem is solved affirmatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: pick any Latin square L of order n and orient horizontal edges from smaller to larger entry and vertical edges from larger to smaller entry; this yields d+(v) = n − 1 for all vertices. Apply Lemma 1: every induced subgraph corresponds to a bipartite graph and by Lemma 2 that bipartite graph has a stable matching which gives a kernel; hence a list coloring exists. The proof is constructive: orientation derived from a Latin square + stable matching argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-graph generalization (line graphs of bipartite graphs are list-colorable with χ = χ_l)
rubrics_metrics.description: If H is the line graph L(G) of a bipartite graph G, then χ(H) = χ_l(H); in particular the method for S_n (the line graph of K_{n,n}) adapts to show equality for such line graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof adapts Galvin's method: interpret vertices of H as edges of a bipartite graph and use orientations induced by an edge-labeling (Latin-square-like) plus the existence of stable matchings to produce kernels. This yields that list-chromatic number equals ordinary chromatic number for line graphs of bipartite graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thomassen's theorem (5-list-colorability of planar graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every planar graph G is 5-choosable: χ_l(G) ≤ 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to near-triangulated planar graphs (add edges). Use a stronger inductive statement: for a near-triangulated graph with outer cycle B where two adjacent vertices x,y on B are precolored different colors α,β, require |C(v)| ≥ 3 for other vertices on B and |C(v)| ≥ 5 for interior vertices; then the precoloring extends to a list-coloring of G. Induction splits on whether B has a chord (split into two smaller near-triangulated graphs) or not (delete a boundary-adjacent interior vertex v0, reserve two colors γ,δ from C(v0), remove γ,δ from lists of adjacent vertices, then apply induction and choose γ or δ for v0 avoiding neighbor's color). This is a constructive, inductive method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art gallery theorem (Chvátal/Fisk): n/3 guards suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: For a simple polygon (museum) with n walls (vertices) ⌊n/3⌋ guards stationed at vertices suffice to see every point of the polygon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof (Fisk): triangulate the polygon (n−3 non-crossing diagonals). The triangulation graph is 3-colorable (prove by induction splitting along a diagonal). One color class has size at most ⌊n/3⌋; placing guards at vertices of that color class guarantees every triangle contains a guard, so the whole polygon is guarded. This gives an explicit placement method by triangulation then 3-coloring.
